title: Align Value, Profit, and People Propositions
hook: A sold-out lunch counter can still fail if the cooks hate the new promise.
counterintuition: The hidden cost is misalignment among buyer value, profit, and people incentives, where one strong proposition can be weakened by the other two.
tryThisNow: Write one sentence each for buyer value, profit logic, and people support for a current idea. Underline the weakest sentence.
keyTakeaway: Sustainable blue ocean strategy aligns the value proposition, profit proposition, and people proposition so buyers want it, the model pays, and the people system can deliver.

breakdown.fastRead: At 12:17, Beata's lunch counter sells every grain bowl and still loses money because each order takes six custom steps and two cooks skip breaks. Buyer value is real. Profit and people are breaking. Alignment asks a harder question than does the market want it. It asks whether the whole system can keep its promise. A strategy can be popular and still brittle. The three propositions force the team to inspect the kitchen, margin sheet, and partner counter with the same seriousness as the line outside.
breakdown.deepRead:
Beata's first week looks like success from the sidewalk. The line reaches the door. Customers photograph the bowls. Inside, cooks are drowning in custom toppings, labor cost is ugly, and the prep partner refuses the new delivery window.

The value, profit, and people propositions have to fit. The value proposition says why buyers care. The profit proposition says how the organization earns an acceptable return at the strategic price and cost. The people proposition says why employees, partners, and participants have reason and support to execute well.

Nabil's mobile clinic shows the same structure. Patients love evening visits, but the van schedule loses money unless routes cluster, and nurses burn out unless documentation is simplified. The offer is not aligned until all three conditions hold.

A beautiful buyer promise can become an execution debt if the people and profit systems are treated as secondary.

The alignment test should happen before scale, not after strain appears. Ask the cooks, nurses, drivers, partners, support agents, and installers what the promise does to their day. Then ask finance where money is made and lost. The buyer line is only one part of the system speaking.
breakdown.fullRead:
A buyer breakthrough can hide weakness. Teams love to see demand because demand feels like proof. But sustainable strategy has three linked propositions. Buyers need a compelling reason to choose the offer. The organization needs a profit logic that can carry the promise. Employees and partners need a people proposition that makes delivery rational, supported, and fair.

Beata learns this at 12:17 behind a lunch counter. The new grain bowls sell out every day. Customers love picking sauces, seeds, roasted vegetables, and crunch. The value proposition is alive. The profit proposition is bleeding because each bowl takes six custom steps and waste spikes after 1:00. The people proposition is worse. Cooks skip breaks, argue over prep space, and quietly hate the promise the menu makes. The sidewalk says success. The kitchen says misalignment.

Tata Nano is a useful warning here: a striking buyer and profit idea can still stumble when the people side cannot carry the promise cleanly. Alignment does not mean each proposition repeats the same sentence. They answer different questions. Value: why will buyers care enough to change behavior? Profit: how will the firm earn from that choice at a cost structure it can sustain? People: why will the people who must deliver, sell, support, supply, or approve the offer commit their effort?

Nabil's mobile clinic shows the three questions together. Patients value evening visits in apartment courtyards. The profit logic requires clustered routes and fixed visit types, not heroic one-off trips across town. The people proposition requires nurse safety protocols, lighter documentation, and a schedule that does not punish the same team every night. If any one piece fails, the strategy weakens. Patients may want it, but the clinic cannot carry it. Or the economics may work, but nurses refuse the schedule. Or staff may be willing, but patients do not see enough utility to book.

Rosario faces a partner version. Her refillable cleaning-product kiosk saves shoppers money and reduces packaging. The grocery store partner likes the foot traffic but hates sticky spills and slow checkout questions. The people proposition includes the partner's staff. Until Rosario creates sealed cartridges, a cleanup kit, and a margin share for the store, the buyer value sits on top of partner irritation.

The counterargument is that alignment sounds like waiting for perfection. It is not perfection. It is coherence. Early versions can be rough, but the roughness must be visible in the right places. A team can pilot with low volume while learning cost. It can support staff manually before automation. It can compensate partners during a test. What it cannot do is call buyer enthusiasm a complete strategy while the model and people system quietly reject the offer.

Use three separate scorecards. Do not let a strong value proposition bully the other two into silence. Ask where money is made, where cost is removed, who must change behavior, and what they receive in return. A blue ocean grows stronger when the promise, economics, and human system reinforce each other instead of fighting in the back room.

examples.title: Beata sells out while the cooks miss breaks

planSpec.domain: grain bowl lunch counter with buyer demand but weak profit and people fit
planSpec.audience: a food operator whose popular offer strains the kitchen
planSpec.stakes: whether a successful menu can survive the system behind it
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees that buyer value alone is not enough when cost and cooks break

examples.scenario: Beata stands at 12:17 p.m. beside the grain-bowl line, sauce bottles sticky under her palms. The counter sells out by one every day. Customers love the six topping choices. In the kitchen, two cooks have missed breaks again, quinoa waste is filling a bus tub, and labor cost is wrecking the margin sheet clipped by the register. Beata is about to add a seventh topping because buyers asked. She must decide whether demand is proof or only one proposition passing.
examples.whatToDo: Freeze new toppings. Redesign the bowls around fewer prep paths, visible buyer value, workable margin, and a cook schedule people can live with.
examples.whyItMatters: Buyer enthusiasm can hide profit and people failure. The strategy holds only if the promise pays and the people system can deliver it repeatedly.

examples.title: Nabil clusters the evening clinic route before adding vans

planSpec.domain: mobile clinic evening visits aligned with route economics and nurse workload
planSpec.audience: a clinic leader excited by demand for evening visits
planSpec.stakes: whether the service scales without losing money or burning out nurses
planSpec.requiredBeat: he chooses route clustering and documentation redesign before expanding

examples.scenario: Nabil sits in the mobile clinic van at 8:42 p.m., the dashboard glowing blue while a nurse finishes notes in the passenger seat. Patients love evening courtyard visits. The route map on his tablet zigzags across twelve miles for four appointments, and the nurse has not eaten since noon. A donor has offered money for a second van. Nabil's thumb hovers over the reply. He has to decide whether to scale demand or align the route, cost, and nurse proposition first.
examples.whatToDo: Cluster routes, narrow visit types, and simplify documentation before adding capacity. Make the model workable for patients, margins, and nurses together.
examples.whyItMatters: Scaling a misaligned offer multiplies strain. The value proposition needs a profit path and a people proposition before expansion makes sense.

examples.title: Rosario wipes soap from the partner store floor

planSpec.domain: refill kiosk partner staff burden and people proposition
planSpec.audience: a sustainability entrepreneur selling through grocery partners
planSpec.stakes: whether partners keep the kiosk after early shopper interest
planSpec.requiredBeat: she traces a promising buyer offer to partner irritation and redesigns the staff proposition

examples.scenario: Rosario kneels at 9:25 p.m. with brown paper towels, wiping lavender soap from the grocery store floor after the refill kiosk's first Saturday. Shoppers liked the lower price. The store manager did not like sticky aisles, checkout questions, and staff losing ten minutes per spill. Rosario had called the store a channel, not a people proposition. Now the mop bucket beside her says otherwise.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign for the partner staff: sealed cartridges, spill kit, clearer labels, margin share, and a support number before expanding to another store.
examples.whyItMatters: Partners execute the promise in front of buyers. If their work gets worse with no return, the strategy loses a necessary human link.

examples.title: Irina asks who pays for the cheap printer ink

planSpec.domain: family printer value promise and honest profit model
planSpec.audience: a product lead tempted by a popular low-price device
planSpec.stakes: whether a low-friction buyer offer can make money without hidden traps
planSpec.requiredBeat: she challenges a value proposition that has no honest profit model

examples.scenario: Irina holds a plastic printer shell at 3:14 p.m. while the product team cheers the prototype price. "Families will love it," the designer says. Irina taps the ink cartridge bay with a pencil. "And where do we earn without making them hate us later?" The room goes quiet. The old market made money by punishing refills. The new promise is easy printing for school nights. Irina has to decide how to answer profit without betraying value.
examples.whatToDo: Build profit around transparent subscription, lower service cost, or bundled school supplies, not a hidden refill trap that destroys the buyer promise.
examples.whyItMatters: A profit proposition that contradicts buyer value will pull the strategy back into the old market logic.

examples.title: Jae labels the lockers before asking aides to stay late

planSpec.domain: library after-hours pickup aligned with staffing
planSpec.audience: a civic manager trying to expand access after hours
planSpec.stakes: whether after-hours pickup works without unpaid staff strain
planSpec.requiredBeat: the first plan gave patrons value but asked staff to absorb hidden work, then lockers and shifts aligned it

examples.scenario: Before 5:00 p.m., Jae's after-hours library pickup plan depended on aides staying late to sort holds by hand. Patrons loved the idea. Staff hated the invisible overtime. After one failed week, Jae installed numbered lockers, cut two low-use desk hours, and rotated one paid closing shift. The first patron opened locker 14 at 7:06 with a paperback and no apology owed to anyone.
examples.whatToDo: Align access with staffing. Use lockers, shift changes, and cuts to low-use hours so patron value does not depend on unpaid goodwill.
examples.whyItMatters: People alignment turns a good public promise into a service that can repeat without resentment.

examples.title: Manuela predicts dog owners will pay for calm

planSpec.domain: quiet dog-wash service tested against groomer strain and margin
planSpec.audience: a small business owner testing a quieter grooming format
planSpec.stakes: whether a high-value experience works for owners, groomers, and margins
planSpec.requiredBeat: she predicts value is enough, then groomer strain and cost force alignment

examples.scenario: Manuela opens the quiet dog-wash room at 10:38 a.m. with rubber mats, warm towels, and no dryers screaming. Owners of anxious dogs sign up fast. She predicts the calm format will sell itself. By noon, the groomer's back aches from slower hand drying, towel laundry is piling up, and the price barely covers labor. Manuela watches a terrier stop shaking in the tub. Manuela has to decide whether to raise the price, redesign the labor, or stop calling buyer demand a complete proposition.
examples.whatToDo: Keep calm as the buyer promise, but redesign drying tools, session length, price, and groomer rotation until value, profit, and people fit.
examples.whyItMatters: A humane offer still needs economics and staff support. Alignment protects the promise from collapsing under delivery costs.

questions.prompt: A manager at a meal service has customers praising a custom menu, but cooks hate the process and margins are negative. Which diagnosis is strongest? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: The value proposition works, but profit and people propositions are misaligned.
The strategy is complete because buyers are happy.
The cooks should be ignored because customers matter most.
questions.explanation: Buyer demand is one condition. The model also needs workable economics and a people system capable of delivery.

questions.prompt: A founder creates a low-cost tutoring offer parents love, but tutors lose unpaid prep time every night. What should she do? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: Add more students quickly to exploit demand.
Redesign pricing, materials, and tutor workflow so the people proposition supports the buyer promise.
Tell tutors the mission should be enough.
questions.explanation: The people proposition is failing. Growth will worsen delivery unless tutors receive support, time, or incentives aligned with the offer.

questions.prompt: A director at a refill store earns margin by making replacement parts confusing and expensive, even though the buyer promise is simplicity. What is wrong? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: The people proposition is too generous.
The store has too many partners.
The profit proposition contradicts the value proposition.
questions.explanation: Profit logic that punishes the buyer undermines the promise. Alignment requires earning money in a way that supports value.

questions.prompt: A manager at a clinic wants to expand evening care. Patients want it, but nurses fear unsafe solo visits. Which proposition needs design? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: People proposition for the staff delivering the service.
Only the buyer proposition.
Only brand positioning.
questions.explanation: Staff safety and support are part of the people proposition. Without it, execution will resist the offer.

questions.prompt: A designer at a software company has a feature users want and a profitable price, but customer support will face twice the ticket volume with no tools. Which action aligns the move?
choices: Launch and let support catch up.
Add support tooling, training, or product simplification before scaling.
Cut support from the plan to protect margin.
questions.explanation: Support is part of the people system. The strategy needs delivery capacity, not only buyer appeal and price.

questions.prompt: A coach starts a low-cost travel team parents love, but volunteer drivers carry all weekend burden. What is the alignment issue? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: The value proposition is irrelevant because sports teams need sacrifice.
The profit proposition is the only thing that matters.
The people proposition for volunteers is weak and may break the offer.
questions.explanation: Volunteers are required participants. If their burden is unsupported, the offer will not sustain.

questions.prompt: A manager at a bookstore creates a popular same-day school reading bundle. What question checks profit alignment? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: Can the store assemble and price the bundle at a margin that survives rush orders?
Do rival stores have nicer shelves?
Can every employee name the publisher of each title?
questions.explanation: Profit alignment asks whether the business can earn from the promise at the needed cost and price.

questions.prompt: A director at a nonprofit has strong donor enthusiasm but frontline staff say the new promise creates impossible reporting work. What should happen before launch?
choices: Treat staff concerns as negativity.
Align reporting demands, staffing, and incentives with the donor promise.
Launch faster so staff adapt under pressure.
questions.explanation: Donor value does not replace people alignment. Reporting work is part of delivery and must be designed.

questions.prompt: A student venture wants to judge a strategy in one meeting. Which three questions should structure it? The team has one week before the budget review and must choose the next move now.
choices: What do buyers want, what do rivals fear, and what sounds impressive?
What is the logo, launch date, and slogan?
Why will buyers care, how will the model pay, and why will people deliver it well?
questions.explanation: Those are the three propositions: value, profit, and people. Together they test sustainability.

reviewCards.front: A buyer offer is popular but delivery feels miserable. What proposition is failing?
reviewCards.back: The people proposition. Identify who must deliver the promise, what burden they carry, and what support or incentive makes delivery rational.

reviewCards.front: Your profit model earns by frustrating buyers later. What should you suspect?
reviewCards.back: Profit and value are misaligned. The business may make money short term while pulling the strategy back toward the old pain it promised to remove.

reviewCards.front: A partner channel likes the revenue but hates the operational mess. How do you include that?
reviewCards.back: Treat the partner as part of the people proposition. The offer must give partner staff tools, clarity, margin, or reduced burden.

reviewCards.front: You have to evaluate a promising strategy fast. What three sentences should you force?
reviewCards.back: Write one sentence for buyer value, one for profit logic, and one for people support. The weakest sentence tells you where the strategy will break.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is proposition alignment. You separate buyer value, profit logic, and people support, then check whether they reinforce or undermine each other. The practice keeps demand from hiding economic or execution debt.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a new offer gets buyer praise, then ask how margin works and who absorbs the delivery burden before approving scale.
If a care plan sounds ideal, then check whether cost, schedule, and caregiver workload make it repeatable.
If a project delights its audience but drains you, then redesign scope, price, or support before adding commitments.
If a shared promise benefits one person and burdens another, then renegotiate the people proposition before resentment sets in.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, take one idea and write three headings: buyer value, profit or resource logic, and people support. Put one risk under each and choose the weakest heading for repair.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Weekly, review one project that is getting praise. Ask whether money, time, partners, and people are aligned with the promise buyers like.

memorableLines.text: A buyer breakthrough can hide weakness.
memorableLines.why: Makes alignment concrete through visible demand and hidden strain, the core tension of the chapter.

memorableLines.text: The sidewalk says success. The kitchen says misalignment.
memorableLines.why: Vivid parallel structure that captures the contrast between visible demand and hidden system failure.

memorableLines.text: A strategy can be popular and still brittle.
memorableLines.why: Compressed principle that flips the reader's assumption: popularity does not guarantee durability without alignment.
